btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The interagency Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models - finalized by FHFA, CFPB, and the banking regulators - are the first binding federal rules for the sector's core AI: the models that value homes in mortgage decisions.
points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.desc: The bureau's AVM rule page and its algorithmic-appraisal work are the record of how valuation bias and model accountability are supervised.
points.name: CFPB carries the consumer-protection side

points.name: Opendoor prices houses with models at risk

points.name: Leasing and property ops are automating

points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.desc: The Building Owners and Managers Association tracks AI in smart-building operations, energy efficiency, and predictive maintenance across commercial property.
points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.desc: The realtor association's technology accelerator is where residential proptech gets vetted and scaled - a window into which tools the profession is actually adopting.
points.name: NAR REACH backs the startups

points.desc: The residential brokerage's platform applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and predictive listing recommendations.
points.name: Compass runs AI inside the brokerage workflow

points.desc: HouseCanary's valuation and forecasting models and Cherre's data integration layer are what institutional investors underwrite on - the wholesale side of the AVM story.
points.name: Institutional valuation runs on data platforms

points.name: Lease abstraction is a document-AI problem

points.desc: Visitt and Building Engines apply IoT sensing and machine learning to HVAC optimization, maintenance prediction, and tenant workflow in operating buildings.
points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent measurement period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making it one of the more measurably active sectors in the survey. The increase is gradual but consistent, suggesting that adoption is broadening across firm types rather than being driven by a handful of large operators.

The most established AI application in the sector is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate home valuations for 110 million or more homes using a neural network-based model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and user-submitted data, and the company describes ongoing work to reduce error rates and improve responsiveness to local trends and seasonality. HouseCanary similarly offers AI-powered valuations and forecasts covering over 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning with image recognition technology to assess home condition directly from photos. Opendoor applies pricing models to make direct purchase offers, carrying the valuation risk on its own balance sheet rather than simply providing estimates. On the commercial side, Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from documents and combines the output with expert validation to produce structured lease data, addressing one of the more labor-intensive data problems in commercial real estate portfolio management.

Operational automation is a second major deployment area. EliseAI offers an agentic conversational AI platform that handles inbound messages, calls, tour scheduling, prospect follow-up, and maintenance requests around the clock, with the company positioning the tool as reducing overhead and freeing staff for higher-value work. Building Engines, described as a JLL company, offers an AI-powered property management platform that standardizes portfolio data and provides performance dashboards and actionable recommendations aimed at improving net operating income. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models and integrates with platforms such as Procore and Autodesk, with the company citing reduced site visits and improved portfolio management as operational benefits. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, deploying it across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics, though the sources do not provide a specific dollar figure.

Automated valuation models have become the sector's first category of federally regulated AI. The CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized a rule under the Dodd-Frank Act requiring mortgage originators and secondary market issuers that use AVMs in credit decisions or securitization determinations to maintain quality control standards ensuring high confidence in estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing and review. This rule is the clearest signal that AI in real estate, at least where it touches mortgage collateral valuation, now carries binding compliance obligations rather than voluntary best-practice guidance.

For a decision-maker evaluating deployment, the sourced material points to a sector where the technology is available and demonstrably in use across valuation, leasing communications, document extraction, building operations, and portfolio analytics, but where the regulatory floor is rising. Any AVM used in mortgage decisions now falls under interagency quality-control requirements, and the CFPB's involvement indicates that bias, model accountability, and consumer protection remain active supervisory concerns. The National Association of Realtors and its REACH accelerator provide some visibility into which tools the residential profession is adopting, while CRETI and CREtech serve as indicators of where commercial proptech investment and practitioner attention are concentrating. Organizations considering deployment in document AI, leasing automation, or building operations face a less prescriptive regulatory environment today than those deploying valuation models in lending contexts, though the direction of regulatory travel across the sector is clearly toward greater scrutiny.
